title_en: An Election Day Special With Nate Silver
title_zh: 选举日特别节目：对话 Nate Silver（Silver Bulletin）
subtitle_zh: Joe 与 Tracy 携手 Nate Silver 解读中期选举：民调误差、预测市场与民主党胜算。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 是选举日特别节目，Joe Weisenthal 与 Tracy Alloway 请来 Silver Bulletin 创始人、以 FiveThirtyEight 闻名的 Nate Silver 解读中期选举。Silver 指出 Trump 支持率约 37%、其中仅 19% 为强烈支持，按某些口径是自 Harry Truman（1946 年）以来总统在中期选举时最差；对比 2018 年共和党丢掉 41 个众议院席位，他把本次称为「前有悬崖、后有深坑」的选举：民主党大环境极佳，大概率拿下众议院并夺回部分州长与州议会席位，但要赢参议院须在 Texas、Kansas、Alaska 乃至 South Carolina 这类深红州获胜。节目检验了「对 Trump 的公投」这一先验——证据之一是共和党竞选广告与播客已刻意回避 Trump，而 Trump 本人却想当主角；Silver 也谈到消费者情绪的长期低迷与实际消费支出之间的落差、「数字孪生」（digital twin）民调设想，以及选区重划下的 dummymander 风险。他透露自己的模型与 Polymarket 在各州的相关性高达 0.995，并反思民调机构作为「自身利益相关玩家」正集体自我修正——没人想重演 Ann Selzer 2024 年误判 Iowa 那样的结果。

turns.zh: 这周尤其如此。我们是在 10 月 29 日录的这期，节目会在 11 月 3 日上线。

turns.en: It's a pretty big week for politics. So we should talk, to put it mildly. To put it mildly. I know, I know.
turns.zh: 这对政治来说是相当重要的一周，所以我们应该聊聊，说得委婉一点。说得委婉一点。我知道，我知道。

turns.en: Anyway, let's just jump right to it. Joining us here on our Election Day special, Nate Silver. Everyone knows him. Founder of the Silver Bulletin newsletter, famous for 538, modeling elections, knowing a lot about polling and data and all that stuff. Nate, thank you for joining our Election Day special.
turns.zh: 好了，我们直接进入正题。今天来到我们选举日特别节目的嘉宾是 Nate Silver，大家都认识他。他是 Silver Bulletin 这份 newsletter 的创始人，以 538（FiveThirtyEight）闻名，擅长给选举建模，对民调和数据这些东西非常在行。Nate，感谢你来参加我们的选举日特别节目。

turns.en: Of course. Thanks, Joe. Thanks, Tracy.
turns.zh: 当然。谢谢 Joe，谢谢 Tracy。

turns.en: Let's just talk about like how unpopular is President Trump right now as of October 29th or Election Day and to what degree? I mean, midterms historically pretty bad for the party and power, but just get a big picture. How historically unpopular is President Trump and what is the knock-on effects for various Republican candidates in competitive races?
turns.zh: 我们来聊聊，截至 10 月 29 日、或者说选举日，Trump 总统现在有多不受欢迎，程度如何？我是说，中期选举历史上对执政党一般都挺不利的，但先给个大致的图景。Trump 总统在历史上有多不受欢迎，这又会对那些选情胶着的共和党候选人产生什么样的连锁影响？

turns.en: Yeah. So Trump's approval rating is at about 37 percent. By some measures, that's the worst approval rating for a president at a midterm since Harry Truman, I think, in 1946. I'm getting that right. And remember we had a midterm in 2018 where Trump and Republicans lost 41 House seats when he was somewhat less unpopular and where gas didn't cost $ 4. 30 a gallon or whatever it is. So look. I kind of call this the rock versus the hard place election, right? The background conditions couldn't be better for Democrats, right? The historical trends in midterms, voter anxiety about the economy, the Iran war, Trump's a lame duck and 80 years old. They've done really well. And with turnout, they're doing well in early voting so far. They had a very good year in 2025 with New Jersey and Virginia. It's really very consistent indicators. I mean, they might have a couple of problems. Some of their candidates are seen as too far left, right? So that's kind of the rock. And the hard place is, yeah, they'll probably win the House. They'll probably pick up some governorships and state legislatures, but they do have to win in some really red states, just how the math works, to win the Senate, right? States as red as Texas, Kansas, Alaska, South Carolina is in play, if you believe the polls. And so it's kind of this big, I mean, this is why I like, I would say I'm a little bit anxious, not just for the implication for the country, but because like, it's kind of become a tricky race for like models and polls and forecasts, right? There's no... There's no gimme. You either have to lie and say it's a toss-up. That's not an honest answer at this point, right? That's hedging.
turns.zh: 嗯。Trump 的支持率大概在 37% 左右。按某些口径算，这是自 Harry Truman 以来——我记得是 1946 年——总统在中期选举时最差的支持率，我没记错的话。而且别忘了 2018 年那次中期选举，Trump 和共和党丢掉了 41 个众议院席位，那时候他还没这么不受欢迎，油价也没到现在这样 4.30 美元一加仑之类的。所以你看，我基本上把这次叫作'前有悬崖、后有深坑'（rock versus the hard place）的选举，对吧？对民主党来说，大环境好得不能再好了：中期选举的历史规律、选民对经济的焦虑、Iran 战争、Trump 是跛脚鸭（lame duck）而且还 80 岁了。他们表现真的很好。投票率方面，他们目前提前投票表现不错，2025 年在 New Jersey 和 Virginia 也是非常好的一年。这些指标真的非常一致。我是说，他们可能也有那么几个问题：有些候选人被认为太偏左了，对吧？这算是那个'悬崖'。而'深坑'是——是的，他们大概率能拿下众议院，大概率能夺回一些州长席位和州议会，但要赢下参议院，按这个数学算法，他们必须在一些非常红的州获胜，对吧？像 Texas、Kansas、Alaska 这么红的州，如果你信民调的话，连 South Carolina 都在争夺范围内。所以这是个很微妙……我是说，这就是为什么——我会说我有点焦虑，不只是为这个国家的影响焦虑，而是因为这对模型、民调和预测来说已经变成一场很难办的选举，对吧？没有……没有那种白送的答案。你要么得撒谎说这是五五开——到这个节点上那已经不是一个诚实的答案了，对吧？那是在和稀泥。

turns.en: But you have to take a kind of leap of faith that the Democrat could win in Texas.
turns.zh: 但你得有那么一点信念之跃（leap of faith），相信民主党可能在 Texas 赢。

turns.en: You have to kind of take a leap of faith on some of this stuff. And a probabilistic leap of faith. But at this point, it would be a really bad night for pollsters if Democrats don't win the Senate.
turns.zh: 这些东西你确实得有点信念之跃，而且是概率意义上的信念之跃。但到了这个节点，如果民主党没赢下参议院，那对民调机构来说会是非常糟糕的一晚。

turns.en: Just to sort of test our priors a little bit. Everyone's treating this as a referendum on Trump, which kind of like makes me nervous when everyone's doing the same thing. But in your view, is that an accurate way to measure it? Like, do we have hardcore evidence that people are voting on Trump rather than voting on a local representative?
turns.zh: 稍微检验一下我们的先验（priors）。大家都把这当成对 Trump 的一次公投，而当所有人都在做同一件事时，这反倒让我有点不安。但在你看来，这是一种准确的衡量方式吗？我们有没有硬核证据表明，人们投票是冲着 Trump，而不是冲着本地的议员？

turns.en: I think the best evidence is that Trump is no longer featured in Republican campaign commercials, right? Trump is not being talked about anymore on Republican podcasts. However, Trump himself is trying to make himself like the main character of this story when I don't think very many Republicans want that, right? Ironically, they had this Republican convention, was it in Dallas just after Labor Day? And like, that's when Republican polls kind of went from bad to worse. I don't think that's the main cause or necessarily even the secondary cause. But yeah, I mean, the behavior you'd expect if people are being kind of game theory optimal is that Trump is taking a back seat and trying to let his more moderate candidates distance themselves a little bit. And instead, we've seen the opposite, right? I mean, if Trump hadn't endorsed Ken Paxton in Texas, I'm not sure that James Tallarico would have a slight lead there. If Trump hadn't chosen to go to war with Iran, I tend to think the Senate would be a toss up and not lean D. So no, he's the central character. And it's also kind of like, It's kind of like the last time Trump is on the ballot, barring extra constitutional shenanigans.
turns.zh: 我觉得最好的证据是：Trump 已经不再出现在共和党的竞选广告里了，对吧？共和党的播客上也不再讨论 Trump 了。然而 Trump 自己却想把自己变成这个故事的主角，而我觉得没多少共和党人希望这样，对吧？讽刺的是，他们开了那个共和党大会——是在 Labor Day 之后、在 Dallas 吧？——就在那时候，共和党的民调开始从糟糕变得更糟。我不觉得那是主因，甚至未必是次因。但是的，我是说，如果大家都按博弈论（game theory）最优来行事，你会预期的行为是 Trump 退居幕后，让他那些更温和的候选人稍微跟他拉开点距离。可我们看到的恰恰相反，对吧？我是说，如果 Trump 没在 Texas 给 Ken Paxton 背书，我不确定 James Talarico 会不会在那里略微领先。如果 Trump 没选择跟 Iran 开战，我倾向于认为参议院会是五五开，而不是偏向民主党。所以不，他就是核心角色。而且这也差不多是——差不多是 Trump 最后一次出现在选票上，除非有什么逾越宪法的幺蛾子。

turns.en: Yeah, which who knows? Now, this gets to the question of like, could it be a bad night for pollsters? And there is this seems to this view has congealed in the general public that starting at least since 2016, pollsters always overestimate Democrats.
turns.zh: 是啊，谁知道呢？这就引出了那个问题：会不会是民调机构糟糕的一晚？而且在公众里似乎已经固化了这么一种看法——至少从 2016 年起，民调机构总是高估民主党。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: I think your view is that that's actually just factually incorrect. But why don't you tell us about what we know about polling error?
turns.zh: 我觉得你的观点是，这在事实上其实是站不住脚的。那你不如给我们讲讲，关于民调误差，我们到底知道些什么？

turns.en: So what we know, number one, is that polling errors are correlated. That if a poll misses high on the Democrat in Iowa, probably in a similar state like Kansas or Nebraska, all three states are competitive this year, good chance you'll have a correlated error. So therefore, you cannot look at individual races as a Monte Carlo random. But A, they're less correlated in midterms than in presidential years because you have different candidates on the ballot in every state. That's important. In 2022, we saw this kind of really big red wave in like New York, New Jersey, tri-state area. And Republicans did really well in Florida. The rest of the map was relatively good for Democrats. John Fetterman won and people like that, given that Biden had like a 39% approval rating. You know, number two, we have had systematic polling errors that underestimated Trump in 2016, 2020, 2024, a little bit more modest, but still direction the same, right? In every election in the Trump era where Trump is not on the ballot, You have not had that error. And in fact, in like New Jersey and Virginia last year, you had a massive underestimation of Democrats and governors races. And so like, first of all, it could all be noise, right? If you like code up a, you know, have Claude or whatever, or GPT code up a SIM to just show you like what random polling error looks like in the past 20 elections, it looks kind of like, you know, it's impossible to distinguish it.
turns.zh: 我们知道的第一点是，民调误差是相关的。如果在 Iowa，某份民调把民主党估高了，那么在类似的州——比如 Kansas 或 Nebraska，这三个州今年都有竞争——很可能你会得到一个相关的误差。因此，你不能把每一场单独的选战都当成 Monte Carlo（蒙特卡洛）式的随机事件。但是，第一，中期选举里的相关性比总统选举年要弱，因为每个州选票上的候选人都不一样，这点很重要。2022 年，我们在 New York、New Jersey、tri-state（三州）地区看到了相当大的红色浪潮，共和党在 Florida 也表现得非常好，但版图上其余的地方对民主党相对有利，John Fetterman 之类的人赢了，尽管当时 Biden 的支持率只有 39% 左右。第二点，我们确实经历过系统性的民调误差，在 2016、2020、2024 年都低估了 Trump，2024 年幅度稍微小一点，但方向一致，对吧？而在 Trump 时代每一场 Trump 不在选票上的选举里，你都没有出现那种误差。事实上，去年在 New Jersey 和 Virginia 的州长选举里，你还严重低估了民主党。所以说，首先，这一切可能都只是噪声，对吧？如果你写个程序——比如让 Claude 或者 GPT 之类的写个模拟，给你看过去 20 次选举里随机的民调误差长什么样，它看起来就有点像……你根本没法区分。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But one story might be that like Trump has this kind of magical power to attract voters low turnout voters that also happen to be hard for pollsters to reach and where they get screened out as being unlikely voters. Those voters don't seem to want to show up for like a Roger Marshall in Kansas or a Ken Paxton in Texas, right? It seems very, you know, Trump got a lot of young men last year who flipped to 2024, who flipped to him. Young men don't usually turn out in terms of watching the NFL or whatever, right? And like there's a consistent story where like conveniently this problem of like these missing voters aren't an issue if they don't vote.
turns.zh: 但有一种说法可能是：Trump 有种魔力，能吸引那些低投票率的选民，而这些人恰恰又是民调机构很难触达的，还会被筛掉、判定为不太可能投票的选民。这些人似乎并不愿意为 Kansas 的 Roger Marshall 或 Texas 的 Ken Paxton 站出来投票，对吧？你知道，Trump 去年拿到了很多年轻男性的票，这些人在 2024 年转向了他。年轻男性通常不太出来投票，就像他们看 NFL 什么的也一样，对吧？所以有这样一个自洽的说法——很方便地，这些'消失的选民'的问题，只要他们不投票，就不成问题了。

turns.en: This was actually going to be my next question. But like what are you seeing in terms of early signs of turnout? And then what are the chances that a former Trump voter actually votes Democrat rather than just decides not to show up?
turns.zh: 这其实就是我下一个要问的问题。那你在投票率的早期迹象上看到了什么？以及，一个曾经投 Trump 的选民真的去投民主党的概率有多大，而不是干脆决定不出来投票？

turns.en: As compared to general elections or presidential elections, turnout is relatively speaking more important. in midterms. Differential turnout is almost always a factor in some of these bigger waves. I'm not an early voting expert, but there are people who are pretty good at it, right? It can be very ad hoc if you don't kind of set clear rules ahead of time. And they seem to be seeing good numbers for Democrats, better numbers in the polls. I don't know, because the polls are really good for Democrats, right? But it provides some more consensus evidence for it, particularly high turnout among Black voters who may fear being disenfranchised. high turnout or not high turnout, but comparatively high turnout among unlikely voters, people who in the voter files have voted no more than one in the past four elections. Democrats are getting a lot of those, but they're getting more than Republicans, right? I think some pollsters are finding there's very little D to R crossover. If you're any type of Democrat at all, this is not the year to indulge in a moderate Republican, right? Maybe a little bit of the reverse. But like, I mean, things tell a consistent story. It's just kind of this existential thing about whether people believe the story or not.
turns.zh: 跟大选或总统选举相比，投票率（turnout）在中期选举里相对更重要。差异化的投票率几乎总是那些较大浪潮中的一个因素。我不是提前投票方面的专家，但有些人在这方面相当在行，对吧？如果你不提前设定清晰的规则，这事就会变得很随意。他们似乎看到民主党的数字不错——比民调里更好。我不确定，因为民调对民主党已经非常有利了，对吧？但这提供了一些更具共识性的证据，尤其是黑人选民的高投票率，他们可能担心被剥夺投票权；还有不太可能投票的选民——就是那些在选民档案里、过去四次选举中投票不超过一次的人——他们不是绝对意义上的高投票率，而是相对来说较高的投票率。民主党拿到了很多这样的选民，而且比共和党拿得多，对吧？我觉得有些民调机构发现，民主党转投共和党的情况非常少。只要你多少算是个民主党人，今年就不是去纵容一个温和派共和党的年份，对吧？也许反过来倒是有一点。但我是说，各项信息讲的是一个一致的故事。问题只是那种根本性的：人们到底信不信这个故事。

turns.en: Why is Trump so unpopular? Like, is it just gas and diesel prices? Like, break down the drivers of his unpopularity.
turns.zh: 为什么 Trump 这么不受欢迎？是因为汽油和柴油价格吗？给我们拆解一下他不受欢迎背后的驱动因素。

turns.en: Trump is kind of, well, people are bored of him and tired of him, right? I think people are just like, he's been president for, I guess, six years, right? But it feels like 10 years because he was still kind of the dominant figure of that kind of Biden interregnum. You know, he's 80 years old. But no, look, I think the basic story is that he has broken promises. most prominently on cheaper gas and on no more stupid wars. We can talk about how much the Epstein stuff affects him too. But yeah, one of the things about Trump's reporting number is like, of that 37% approval, like only 19% of it is like strong approval. I think there are permission structures that have opened up for Republicans to kind of distance themselves from Trump and incentives, right? You know, Trump, his endorsement will still matter after 2026, but like, you know, J.D. Vance and Marco Rubio, who are nominally leading candidates, have a big problem in that they kind of are, when Bush was this unpopular in 2026, and it got worse, by the way, after the 06 midterm, you didn't have Dick Cheney trying to run for president, right? You had a rebellious Republican in John McCain who ultimately got nominated instead. And so, you know, when you're a lame duck, the bottom can drop out potentially.
turns.zh: Trump 嘛，嗯，大家对他感到厌烦、也累了，对吧？我觉得大家就是……他当总统，我算算，有六年了吧，对吧？但感觉像十年，因为在 Biden 那段'空窗期'里，他仍然是那种主导性的人物。你知道，他 80 岁了。但不，你看，我觉得基本的故事是他违背了承诺，最突出的就是在更便宜的汽油和'不再打愚蠢的战争'这两点上。我们也可以聊聊 Epstein 那档子事对他的影响有多大。但是的，关于 Trump 这个支持率数字有一点值得说：在那 37% 的支持率里，只有 19% 是强烈支持。我觉得已经出现了一些'许可结构'（permission structures）和动机，让共和党人可以跟 Trump 拉开距离，对吧？你知道，Trump 的背书在 2026 年之后仍然重要，但是，你知道，J.D. Vance 和 Marco Rubio 这两位名义上的领跑候选人有个大问题，那就是——当 Bush 在 2006 年这么不受欢迎时（顺便说一句，06 年中期选举之后还更糟），你并没有看到 Dick Cheney 出来竞选总统，对吧？当时是一个反叛的共和党人 John McCain，最终拿到了提名。所以说，你知道，当你是个跛脚鸭的时候，底可能一下子就塌掉。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: So at the moment when we're recording this, if you look at, I guess, the polling consensus and prediction markets, it seems like the House is pretty much a lock. Senate is a toss up at the moment. What's the actual range of outcomes for a Democratic win here? Like, what are the extremes that you could possibly see on both sides?
turns.zh: 在我们录这期的当下，如果你看民调共识和预测市场（prediction markets），众议院似乎基本已经十拿九稳，参议院目前是五五开。那么民主党获胜的结果，实际的范围有多大？两边你可能看到的极端情形分别是什么？

turns.en: I would push back on the Senate being a toss up. I think at Pauline Marquette and Kelshi, Democrats are up to like 68 percent or something as when we're recording this. And in our model, they're at 70, high 70s now?
turns.zh: 我要反驳一下'参议院五五开'这个说法。我觉得在 Polymarket 和 Kalshi 上，截至我们录制时，民主党赢的概率已经到了 68% 左右。而在我们的模型里，他们现在是 70%、接近 70 后段？

turns.en: To win the Senate.
turns.zh: 赢下参议院的概率。

turns.en: For the Senate?
turns.zh: 参议院？

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Oh, wow. Well, there's this kind of, both a blessing and a curse is to actually have to put out a forecast in the form of a probability, right? Because it'd be easy to say, oh, things are looking good for Democrats. but don't get your hopes up too much because polls can be wrong. And yeah, I guess it leans down, right? Like that's chickening out though.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。嗯，这既是福气也是诅咒——就是你真的得以一个概率的形式给出预测，对吧？因为说'哦，民主党看起来不错，但别抱太大希望，因为民调可能出错'很容易。是啊，我猜它是偏向民主党（leans D），对吧？不过那其实是在打退堂鼓、和稀泥。

turns.en: Like the thing is, it's like, we could all do that. Like this is, I guess, like part of what's interesting about modelers and what's interesting about prediction markets is We could all say, yeah, it looks like Democrats, like if you're going to provide value as the creator of a model, you got to be able to say something beyond it looks like a good night for Democrats, but who knows?
turns.zh: 问题就在于，那种话我们谁都会说。我想这部分正是建模者和预测市场有意思的地方——我们都可以说'是啊，看起来像民主党'。但如果你作为一个模型的创建者要提供价值，你就得能说点比'看起来是民主党的一个好夜晚，但谁知道呢'更实质的东西。

turns.en: And look, in 2024, like our model literally was 50-50. Like literally we ran 80,000 simulations and it took like the 71,000 simulation for one candidate to go ahead, right? So there are times when the correct modeling position is like, oh, people are too sure of themselves. I'm not sure if this is that election, right? If you go and look at Republican-sponsored polls or go look at where Republicans are spending their time and their resources, and they're bracing for a landslide, right? They are doing telehauls and the Louisiana Senate race and things like that, right? And seem concerned about South Carolina, let alone Texas, who people kind of knew would be a competitive race. But, you know, Democrats, I think, felt like they have been betrayed.
turns.zh: 而且你看，2024 年我们的模型真的就是五五开。真的，我们跑了 80,000 次模拟，直到大概第 71,000 次模拟才有一个候选人领先，对吧？所以有时候，正确的建模立场就是'哦，大家太自信了'。我不确定这次是不是那样的选举，对吧？如果你去看共和党自己赞助的民调，或者看共和党把时间和资源花在哪里——他们是在为一场大胜做准备，对吧？他们在 Louisiana 的参议院选战里搞电话市政厅会议（tele-town halls）之类的，对吧？而且似乎对 South Carolina 都很担心，更别说 Texas 了——大家本来就知道 Texas 会是一场有竞争的选战。但是，你知道，民主党这边，我觉得他们感觉自己被辜负了。

turns.en: Is there a Senate race in Louisiana this year?
turns.zh: 今年 Louisiana 有参议院选战吗？

turns.en: There is. I don't think there's been a single poll of it. But prediction markets say there's a 10% chance that Democrats will win that race, right? I think it's a little ridiculous.
turns.zh: 有。我觉得那儿一份民调都没做过。但预测市场说民主党赢下那场的概率有 10%，对吧？我觉得这有点离谱。

turns.en: But that's not nothing. The point is that's far from trivial.
turns.zh: 但那也不是零啊。重点是，那远不是无关紧要的。

turns.en: No, we've had to learn these details about these very red states. Like, oh, South Carolina was a Trump plus 18 state. That's what I'm a little bit more skeptical.
turns.zh: 不，我们不得不去了解这些非常红的州的细节。比如，哦，South Carolina 是一个 Trump +18 的州。这就是我比较怀疑的地方

turns.en: About, right?
turns.zh: ……的地方，对吧？

turns.en: But the vicissitudes between what differentiates Kansas from Nebraska and things like that, if the national environment... Is as polls say it is. Yeah. Democrats are ahead by about nine points on the generic ballot, which are national polls, essentially.
turns.zh: 但 Kansas 和 Nebraska 之间的差别、诸如此类的微妙之处——如果全国大环境真像民调说的那样。是的，民主党在 generic ballot（通用选战民调，本质上就是全国性民调）上领先大约 9 个百分点。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: At nine points, Republicans, there's too much of a headwind for Republicans.
turns.zh: 在 9 个百分点的差距下，共和党面临的逆风太大了。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And like, you know, you can predict exactly which winning tickets Democrats would draw. But the GOP has to be that spread.
turns.zh: 而且你知道，你能说准民主党会抽到哪几张中奖的彩票，但共和党必须得每一张都中才行。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Or it just gets too difficult. difficult and like i think part of the problem with mental models versus actual models right people say well i can easily see this case where there's a bust again in the polls in the midwest right and i can see this case where sure the polls are basically right and polls are a little cautious and democrats have a sweep right and people kind of like wait those 50 50 but first of all there are the messy middle in between stories and like if you have a lead in the polls then you kind of muddle through half the time right it's like an nfl game where you have a field goal lead at halftime and then lots of penalties and turnovers, right? And you wind up winning by a field goal, right? So it's ugly, but Democrats tend to win the ugly races. And like, there is more evidence, including non-polling evidence consistent with the Democrats have a big night story. Like if you just talked about the things we already talked about in the first 15 minutes about gas and Trump approval ratings and Iran and all that stuff, right? You know, it's not a case where you have this clash really between indicators.
turns.zh: 要么就是它变得太难了。太难了。而且我觉得'心智模型'（mental models）跟'真实模型'之间的部分问题就在于：人们会说'哦，我很容易想到这种情形——中西部（Midwest）的民调又爆冷'，对吧；'我也能想到那种情形——民调基本是对的、只是稍微保守了一点，然后民主党全胜'，对吧。于是大家就想'等等，这不就是五五开吗？'。但首先，中间还有一堆乱七八糟的中间情形；而且如果你在民调里领先，那么有一半的时间你就是能混过去，对吧？就像一场 NFL 比赛，你半场时领先一个任意球（field goal），然后一堆犯规和失误，对吧，最后你还是以一个任意球的优势赢了，对吧？所以过程很难看，但民主党往往能赢下这种难看的比赛。而且，有更多的证据——包括非民调的证据——跟'民主党会大赢一晚'这个故事是一致的。就像我们前 15 分钟已经聊到的那些：汽油、Trump 的支持率、Iran 等等，对吧？你知道，这并不是那种各项指标之间真的互相打架的情况。

turns.en: I feel like we've been talking about this for many, many years now, but there's this persistent tension between all the consumer sentiment surveys where people report how they're feeling about the economy. Those have been very bad for many years now versus the actual numbers in the economy on consumer spending and other things that look pretty good. Do you have a story you tell yourself as a forecaster, a story to explain that discrepancy?
turns.zh: 我觉得这事儿我们已经聊了很多很多年了，但一直存在这么一种持续的张力：一边是所有那些消费者情绪调查——人们报告自己对经济的感受，这些年一直非常糟糕；另一边是经济里的实际数字，比如消费支出等等，看起来还挺不错。作为一个预测者，你有没有一套自己讲给自己听的说法，来解释这种落差？

turns.en: Slightly hot take. I think some of the consumer confidence polling is not very good. You know, the good thing about election polls— I don't think.
turns.zh: 算是个有点争议的观点（hot take）吧。我觉得一些消费者信心（consumer confidence）民调做得并不好。你知道，说到选举民调的好处——我可不这么觉得。

turns.en: That's a hot take, by the way. Like, we've been talking about it for a while.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，这确实是个争议观点。这个话题我们已经聊了一阵了。

turns.en: The pollsters are not good. They're not doing best practices at polling.
turns.zh: 你是说民调机构做得不好？他们没有采用民调的最佳实践（best practices）？

turns.en: We had an article that's been published by a guest author named Joel Wertheimer, who.
turns.zh: 我们刊登过一篇文章，作者是一位客座作者，叫 Joel Wertheimer，他……

turns.en: Oh, Joel's been on our podcast.
turns.zh: 哦，Joel 上过我们的播客。

turns.en: He's great. Yeah, and clearly, I think the University of Michigan survey changed the composition to online in a way that just has, like, way too many Democrats in the sample. So, like, ironically, like— Ironically, like— The complaint that people make about election pollsters, which is more or less false, we can talk about that more, is kind of true of these consumer sentiment surveys that like, for better or worse, election polls get a dose of reality every two years. Election polls are made in an environment where pollsters are actively fearful of missing, particularly missing high on Democrats, right? So that's why like, that's why people talk about like, what's the difference between like polls and prediction markets? Polls kind of are prediction markets, right? or polling averages are at least, right?
turns.zh: 他很棒。是啊，而且很明显，我觉得 University of Michigan 那个调查把采集方式改成了线上，结果样本里的民主党人多得离谱。所以，讽刺的是——讽刺的是——人们对选举民调机构的那个抱怨（说他们高估民主党），其实基本上是站不住脚的，这个我们可以多聊聊；反倒是这些消费者情绪调查有点符合那个抱怨。因为不管好坏，选举民调每两年就会挨一记现实的耳光。选举民调是在这样一个环境里做出来的：民调机构真切地害怕出错，尤其害怕把民主党估高，对吧？所以说，这就是为什么——这就是为什么人们会讨论'民调和预测市场到底有什么区别'。民调其实就有点像是预测市场，对吧？或者说，民调平均值（polling averages）至少是，对吧？

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: A poll is a data-informed opinion at this point, right?
turns.zh: 到了今天，一份民调其实就是一个有数据支撑的观点（data-informed opinion），对吧？

turns.en: Because you have to weight it.
turns.zh: 因为你得给它加权（weight）。

turns.en: The pollster has to do so much modeling, right? Is this what you're getting at?
turns.zh: 民调机构必须做大量的建模，对吧？你想说的是这个意思吗？

turns.en: So like Marist released a poll of Maine last week, and the top line number, let me see if I'm getting this right in my head, said Troy Jackson, the Democrat in Maine, is up nine points, which would be a very good result for Democrats. The average, our average, had been like D plus three in that state, right? That's their registered voter poll. They applied a likely voter model that brought that lead down to plus two.
turns.zh: 比如说 Marist 上周发布了一份 Maine 的民调，那个头条数字——让我想想我记得对不对——说 Maine 的民主党人 Troy Jackson 领先 9 个百分点，这对民主党来说会是非常好的结果。而平均值，我们的平均值，在那个州之前大概是民主党 +3，对吧？那是他们的登记选民（registered voter）民调。他们又套用一个可能选民（likely voter）模型，把领先幅度降到了 +2。

turns.en: People self-correct for the Democratic.
turns.zh: 他们是在自我修正民主党的

turns.en: Bias, right? Yeah, there's no way. First of all, the math, just I don't want to get too deep in the weeds, even though it's odd lots. Like the math doesn't, the math doesn't make sense, right? They decided what result they felt comfortable with and reverse engineered.
turns.zh: ……偏差（bias），对吧？是啊，这不可能。首先，这个数学——我不想钻得太深，虽然这可是 Odd Lots（'钻牛角尖'的双关）。就是这个数学、这个数学讲不通，对吧？他们是先决定了自己觉得舒服的结果，再倒推回去的。

turns.en: You see, we just, okay, we don't have to get into the math. But what you're saying is they had a poll that said Troy Jackson was up 9%. But in our likely voter model, it's 2%. And what Nate Silver is saying is like, I don't know how you got from nine to two.
turns.zh: 你看，我们……好吧，我们不必深究那个数学。但你说的是，他们有一份民调显示 Troy Jackson 领先 9%，可一套上他们的可能选民模型，就变成 2%。Nate Silver 的意思是：我不知道你是怎么从 9 变到 2 的。

turns.en: No. And the governor's race went from 11 to zero. Like the math literally doesn't add up. And like, so it's like, okay, so this is your poll and this is your opinion.
turns.zh: 对。而且州长那场从 11 变到了 0。这个数学根本对不上。所以就是说，好吧，这是你的民调，也是你的观点。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Is the way I see it. And like, and we're aggregating opinions. And so like on the one hand, when you see a poll like that, I'm like, I have existential doubt about the accuracy of polling for sure.
turns.zh: 这就是我的看法。而且我们是在聚合这些观点。所以一方面，当你看到那样的民调时，我会想：我对民调的准确性确实存在根本性的怀疑。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: On the other hand, if you have a model that's like a consensus model, thermometer that looks at the correlations and translates poles into probabilities. Like, that's really what Flipper, my model, is doing. And, like, so, like, oh, actually, I kind of like that from a modeling standpoint because it proves the kind of underlying hypothesis that, like, polsters are rational actors and, therefore, although poles are imprecise instruments, there is a lot of incentive not to systematically miss. I got it.
turns.zh: 但另一方面，如果你有一个模型，像一个共识模型、一支温度计，去看这些相关性、把民调转化成概率——这正是 Flipper，也就是我的模型在做的事。所以，哦，其实从建模的角度我还挺喜欢这一点的，因为它验证了那个底层的假设：民调机构是理性的行为者，因此，尽管民调是不精确的工具，他们却有很强的动机不去系统性地估错。明白了。

turns.en: So what you're saying is because you can look at the math and say, look, You can't really justify turning a plus nine into a plus two as someone who aggregates polls and then creates a model that can give you some sort of confidence that like.
turns.zh: 所以你的意思是，因为你能看这个数学、然后说'你看，你没法真正把 +9 变成 +2 说得通'——作为一个聚合民调、再据此建模的人，这能让你对某种东西有信心，比如……

turns.en: Confidence that the errors in the long run, if you have elections every two or four years, will never have data to prove it. But confident that the errors are symmetric in the forecast.
turns.zh: 有信心认为，长远来看——如果每两年或四年才有一次选举，你永远不会有数据去证明它——但有信心认为，预测里的误差是对称的（symmetric）。

turns.en: Yeah, I get exactly what you're saying. So, OK, people don't pick up the phone like they used to.
turns.zh: 嗯，我完全明白你的意思。那么，好，现在人们不像以前那样接电话了。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: You know, certainly they don't recognize it. And if someone calls me and asks for my political opinion, no way. So then there's this vision. Well, why don't we just create an AI replica of Tracy Alloway and an AI replica of Joe Weisenthal and an AI replica of a high school educated oil worker in Texas and an AI replicated version of a HR professional who works for General Motors in the Detroit suburbs. And we just pull them. And then we don't know. And they're always going to pick up the phone. What's wrong with this?
turns.zh: 你知道，他们肯定不认得来号。而且如果有人打电话来问我的政治观点，门儿都没有。于是就有人提出这么一个设想：我们何不干脆做一个 Tracy Alloway 的 AI 复制品、一个 Joe Weisenthal 的 AI 复制品、一个 Texas 高中学历石油工人的 AI 复制品，还有一个在 Detroit 郊区为 General Motors 工作的 HR 专业人士的 AI 复制版，然后我们就去'调查'他们。这样我们……而且他们永远都会接电话。这有什么问题吗？

turns.en: This is the digital twin idea.
turns.zh: 这就是'数字孪生'（digital twin）的设想。

turns.en: Why don't we just create a digital twin of all America?
turns.zh: 我们何不干脆给整个 America 做一个数字孪生？

turns.en: So the problem is like, and by the way, I think these companies are smart. I know some people that work for them, right? But like polling cannot be outsourced to AI agents, right? Because it's one of the few sources of ground truth that we have anymore, number one. And also the models are kind of, so if you ask a poll to create like a synthetic Hispanic respondent, right? 99% of their synthetic responses Hispanic respondents love soccer. It's a bit like if you ask like Claude to pick a number from zero to 10, like always pick seven. It's a bit like, I mean, this gets into the whole existential thing about how like large language models work and like they're kind of, it's kind of the ideal type or something, but like, but no, we need original data, right? Models like Flipper or prediction markets can aggregate that data, but, but, you know, because like voters aren't all that predictable. You know, I don't even like the kind of slicing and dicing that you see. Oh, the Hispanic vote, right? Well, the Hispanic vote is younger Hispanics and older Hispanics, people who are relatively new to the country and people who have been here for a long time, right? Cuban Americans and Puerto Ricans and Mexican Americans and Dominicans and everything else. And like those groups don't always agree with one another. Sure. And people miss it. Like the Hispanic vote is one of the most swingy demographics in the United States. And so like, yeah, it just gets overly reductive and kind of almost like a snake eating its tail a little bit.
turns.zh: 问题在于——顺便说一句，我觉得这些公司很聪明，我认识一些在里面工作的人，对吧？——但是民调不能外包给 AI 智能体（AI agents），对吧？因为第一，它是我们如今所剩无几的'真实基准'（ground truth）来源之一。而且这些模型有点……如果你让一个民调去造一个合成的拉美裔（Hispanic）受访者，对吧？他们造出来的合成拉美裔受访者里，99% 都爱足球。这有点像你让 Claude 从 0 到 10 里挑个数，它总是挑 7。这有点像……我是说，这就牵扯到大语言模型（large language models）如何运作的整个根本性问题，它们给出的有点像是那种'理想型'（ideal type）之类的东西。但是，不，我们需要原始数据，对吧？像 Flipper 这样的模型或者预测市场可以聚合这些数据，但是，你知道，因为选民其实没那么可预测。你知道，我甚至不喜欢你看到的那种切分。哦，'拉美裔选票'，对吧？可拉美裔选票里，有年轻的拉美裔和年长的拉美裔，有相对新来这个国家的人和已经在这儿待了很久的人，对吧？有 Cuban Americans、Puerto Ricans、Mexican Americans、Dominicans 等等。而这些群体彼此并不总是一致。当然。人们却忽略了这点。拉美裔选票其实是 United States 里最容易摇摆的人群之一。所以，是啊，它就会变得过度简化，甚至有点像一条蛇在吞自己的尾巴。

turns.en: I feel like turnout in particular would be difficult for a digital twin to model? Like maybe you can come up with political preference based on demographics, but like predicting whether someone is actually going to leave the House and vote seems particularly difficult to me. But tell me if I'm wrong.
turns.zh: 我觉得投票率这一项，尤其难以用数字孪生来建模吧？也许你能根据人口特征推算出政治偏好，但预测一个人到底会不会真的出门去投票，在我看来特别难。如果我说错了你告诉我。

turns.en: Yeah, we did a little simulation in South Carolina, which is one of the more surprising races to be polling closely. And, you know, and one more, frankly, be a bit more surprised Democrats won.
turns.zh: 是啊，我们在 South Carolina 做了个小模拟，那是选情意外胶着的选战之一。而且，你知道，坦白讲，如果民主党赢了，我会更惊讶一点。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But like, you know, what if black voters in South Carolina turned out at 2024 rates and white voters turn out at 2022 rates, like that shifts the top lines by like 10 points, right? It's a deliberately extreme example. And in South Carolina, the white vote is very conservative. But, you know, that's an example of like, you know, because you have had some midterms where 2018 in particular, you had some states getting up to presidential type turnout. But if it's differential turnout, that would you need that for a state like South Carolina to flip.
turns.zh: 但是，你知道，如果 South Carolina 的黑人选民以 2024 年的投票率出来、而白人选民以 2022 年的投票率出来，那会把头条数字挪动大约 10 个百分点，对吧？这是我故意举的一个极端例子。在 South Carolina，白人选票非常保守。但是，你知道，这就是一个例子——因为你确实经历过一些中期选举，尤其是 2018 年，有些州的投票率能接近总统选举的水平。但如果是差异化投票率（differential turnout），那正是让 South Carolina 这样的州翻盘所需要的东西。

turns.en: The Democrats have 14 percent in Mississippi. on polymarket.
turns.zh: 在 Polymarket 上，民主党在 Mississippi 有 14%。

turns.en: Yeah, that one's a little weird.
turns.zh: 是啊，那个有点奇怪。

turns.en: These are funny states. These southern states are pretty funny, right? Because the top line votes are actually offered frequently fairly close. It's just that every white is a Republican and all the non-whites are not Republicans. And so while it looks really close, it's just like, it's just purely demographics.
turns.zh: 这些州很有意思。这些南方州相当有意思，对吧？因为头条的票数其实经常显示得相当接近。只不过每个白人都投共和党，而所有非白人都不投共和党。所以尽管看起来很接近，其实……纯粹就是人口结构（demographics）决定的。

turns.en: No, so we have a concept in our model that we call elasticity, which is how sensitive is a state to changes in the national race. And that's based on voter-level microdata where we see people clustered at the tails or more in the middle. And, you know, South Carolina, but especially like Louisiana, Mississippi, have very low elasticity. So that's why. So we are lower than polymarket and Democrats in those states.
turns.zh: 不，是这样，我们的模型里有一个概念，叫'弹性'（elasticity），指的是一个州对全国选情变化有多敏感。这是基于选民层面的微观数据（microdata），我们能看到人们是聚集在两端还是更靠中间。而 South Carolina，尤其是 Louisiana、Mississippi，弹性都非常低。所以这就是原因。因此在这些州，我们给民主党的概率比 Polymarket 要低。

turns.en: Actually, since you mentioned demographics, can we talk about gerrymandering for a second? So to what degree do you see that, I guess, backfiring on the Republicans at this point?
turns.zh: 其实，既然你提到人口结构，我们能聊一下选区重划操纵（gerrymandering）吗？那么在多大程度上，你觉得这现在反而在坑共和党自己？

turns.en: So, yeah, a gerrymander where you wind up with fewer seats than you would have under the original maps is a dummymander. Is a term for it?
turns.zh: 是啊，如果一次 gerrymander（选区重划操纵）最后让你拿到的席位比原来那套地图还少，那就叫 dummymander（'蠢划'）。有这么个说法吧？

turns.en: This is an actual term.
turns.zh: 这是个真实存在的术语。

turns.en: It's a term. We have terms for everything in politics. Only poker players have more terms in politics. In Florida, Ron DeSantis drew a map for kind of a presidential year baseline. In presidential years, I expect Florida to remain a pretty red state, right? It's not robust for like a D plus nine climate where Florida goes from R plus 13 to R plus four, right? or something, right? It wasn't designed for that. And if Democrats kind of run the table in Florida, then they could actually wind up with more seats than they would have under the old map, right? In Texas, Republicans hope to make a lot of their gains from, I guess, this maybe frankly arrogant presumption that, oh, now Hispanics in South Texas are now our voters instead of being swingy. And so, like, that probably won't be a dummy mander, but could be a case where the places they hope to maintain gains, you'll have Democratic incumbents holding on.
turns.zh: 是个术语。政治里什么东西我们都有个术语。除了扑克玩家，就数政治里的术语最多了。在 Florida，Ron DeSantis 画的地图基本上是按总统选举年的基准来的。在总统选举年，我预计 Florida 仍会是一个相当红的州，对吧？但它扛不住那种民主党 +9 的大环境——就是 Florida 从共和党 +13 变成共和党 +4 之类的，对吧？这套地图不是为那种情况设计的。如果民主党在 Florida 全面通吃（run the table），那他们最后拿到的席位反而可能比在旧地图下更多，对吧？在 Texas，共和党希望拿到很多斩获，靠的是一种——我觉得坦白说有点自大的假设：哦，现在 South Texas 的拉美裔变成我们的选民了，不再是摇摆的了。所以那大概不会成为一个 dummymander，但也可能出现这样一种情况：在他们指望保住斩获的地方，你会看到民主党的现任议员守住了阵地。

turns.en: Intuitively, if you're a mapmaker... And your only goal is to maximize the number of seats that your party wins. You have to take some risks, right? Is this the key idea here?
turns.zh: 直觉上，如果你是一个画地图的人……而你唯一的目标就是让你自己党赢得的席位最大化，你就必须冒一些风险，对吧？这里的关键点是不是这个？

turns.en: Correct.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: I don't even think they necessarily played it wrong, right? So, you know, again, the House is not quite a sure thing. There is a 5% chance. The way the 5% comes up is that if there is a systematic polling error and the map winds up being a little bit less blue, then the gerrymanders become more effective again, right? So there's like, you know, it's probably not enough for Republicans, but there's like this exponential, there's inflection point at which Joe Mandarin goes from not very helpful to helpful for Republicans.
turns.zh: 我甚至不觉得他们一定玩错了，对吧？所以，你知道，再说一次，众议院并不完全是板上钉钉的事，还有 5% 的概率。这 5% 是这么来的：如果存在系统性的民调误差，版图最后没那么蓝，那么这些 gerrymander 就又会变得有效，对吧？所以说，你知道，这大概不足以帮到共和党，但存在这么一个指数式的、这么一个拐点（inflection point），到了那个点，gerrymander 就从'帮不上什么忙'变成'对共和党有帮助'。

turns.zh: 这里面跟期权（options）市场和凸性（convexity）肯定有某种类比。

But like I think that governor race is really important in part because Abbott is the most prolifically pro data center governor, I think, in the country. And one of the big things I think.
turns.zh: 我觉得州长选举总体上没得到足够的关注。按我们的建模，最后可能有将近三分之二的国土由民主党人主政。但有很多重要的州长选战——跟参议院不一样，参议院里你有很多这种民主党领先一到两个点的情况，而州长这边恰恰相反。Abbott 在 Texas 领先，但只领先几个点。以 Flipper 给出的赔率，我觉得我不会去押 Abbott 输。但我认为那场州长选举真的很重要，部分原因是 Abbott 是我认为全国最积极力挺数据中心（data center）的州长。而且我觉得其中一件大事是……

turns.en: And even he's not that pro data center anymore.
turns.zh: 而且连他都不再那么力挺数据中心了。

But like you're going to have a lot of gridlock. I think the one policy area where you could see action before 28 is on AI, right? I mean, if the timelines are even a third as aggressive as the labs think, then they'll kind of be forced to take action. But I'll be looking for, is there evidence that AI had a big effect in this race and that people were seeing this through pro-AI, got punished for it?
turns.zh: 对。那么假设你至少有国会的一个议院由民主党掌控。也许，你知道，就算民主党只拿到 50 个参议院席位、没真正拿下参议院，但你还是会出现大量的僵局（gridlock）。我觉得在 2028 年之前，唯一可能看到有所行动的政策领域就是 AI，对吧？我是说，如果那些时间表哪怕只有各实验室所认为的三分之一那么激进，那他们某种程度上就会被迫采取行动。而我会关注的是：有没有证据表明 AI 在这次选战中影响很大，以及那些被视为挺 AI（pro-AI）的人是不是因此受到了惩罚？

turns.zh: 可不是，我在看 World Series（世界大赛），结果连着三支广告都是 Mike Lawler 的——就是 Westchester County 那个选区，对吧？我就想，天哪，哪怕在 New York，你也真躲不开。

Spent $ 10 million- or something without his permission on his behalf. It wound up backfiring a little bit.
turns.zh: 但这个体系里的每个人都有动机说广告真的管用。我觉得买广告更好的用法，是提升选民的认知度、并且有可能把版图扩大。但是，你看，有一个关于 Sam Bankman-Fried 的著名故事，我在书里讲过，对吧？不知怎么的，Sam Bankman-Fried 几年前想在 Oregon 的一场众议院初选里力挺一位有效利他主义（effective altruist）的候选人，对吧？然后他给了这人——或者说不是'给'，对吧？——是在未经对方允许的情况下，替他花了大概 1,000 万美元之类的。而那位一度在民调里领先的候选人，最后却惨败，因为我为写书采访了他，他说：选民收到了太多邮件，而且这个给我的竞选砸钱的古怪加密货币亿万富翁到底是谁啊，对吧？结果反而适得其反了一点。

turns.en: This is the flaw in all of advertising, right? Like, you're just annoying me with your product placements and your ads and your intrusion into my life, and it doesn't make me want to buy things from you.
turns.zh: 这就是所有广告的通病，对吧？你就是用你的植入、你的广告、你对我生活的侵入来烦我，而这并不会让我想从你那儿买东西。

turns.en: That's why you need, you know, subscription businesses like terminals and.
turns.zh: 所以你需要的是，你知道，订阅制（subscription）的生意，比如终端（terminals），还有……

turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.zh: 就民主党的内部政治而言，最重要的一场选战可能是 Michigan——Abdul El-Sayed 在初选里击败了更温和的 Haley Stevens，但赢得并不多，并不多。顺便说一句，那场对民调来说不太好看。如果他赢的幅度足够大、大到选举当晚就能宣布结果，那对进步派（progressives）来说就是脸上贴金的一件事。也许像我这样的人会说：'嗯，他只赢了 4 个点，而基准是 9 个点，所以天哪，他表现低于预期，真是个糟糕的候选人。'

turns.zh: 说到 Kansas，我在 Overland Park 有家人，对吧？这么多年一直有种说法，你知道，Roger Marshall 可能会有麻烦，而我基本上从来不太信。就像，喂，那可是 Kansas 啊。但 Kansas 其实已经悄悄地变得更偏民主党了一点。它在这次堕胎公投里投了民主党那一侧，它两次选 Laura Kelly 当州长。你知道，Roger Marshall 有些医疗账单方面的做法非常不光彩。而 Adam Hamilton 主打的就是'哦，我们只是想要更便宜的汽油和正直'——在 Kansas，对吧？这种主打可能正好吃得开。它是一个弹性相对较高的州，对吧？有些民意是可以改变的。它受教育程度也相当高。所以，是啊。而且你知道，上周 CNN 有一份民调显示 Hamilton 在 Kansas 领先 4 个点。但是，是啊，Kansas 算一个。比起 Kansas 的民调，我更难相信的是 South Carolina 的民调。

turns.zh: 不，这其实是一场相当干净的全国性实验。

turns.zh: 而且 Michigan 是个，呃，你知道，他们有一位很强的州长候选人，也是我们在那场选战里看好的人。我不知道是不是有某种程度的衣尾效应（coattails）之类的。但是，是啊，从 11 月 4 日往后，接下来一年半的故事，将会是党内的内斗。

turns.en: What's happening in Florida?
turns.zh: Florida 到底在发生什么？

turns.en: In the Senate race, you had a DSA... Democrat Angie Nixon.
turns.zh: 在参议院那场里，你有一个 DSA 背景的……民主党人 Angie Nixon。

turns.en: Angie Nixon. Oh, she's running for Senate.
turns.zh: Angie Nixon。哦，她在竞选参议员。

turns.en: She's running for Senate, and she's not polling that well. I mean, she's, yeah, Florida, one thing we should probably account for in our models is net domestic migration, right?
turns.zh: 她在竞选参议员，但她民调并不那么好。我是说，她……是啊，Florida——我们的模型里大概应该纳入的一个因素，是净国内移民（net domestic migration），对吧？

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: The models keep missing low on Florida because you have a steady flow of red voters into the state, and we're using benchmarks based on the last election, but Florida's a moving target for that.
turns.zh: 各模型在 Florida 上总是估低，因为一直有稳定的红营选民流入这个州，而我们用的基准是基于上一次选举的，但在这一点上，Florida 是个不断移动的靶子。

turns.en: It's interesting, if you look at polymarkets, because I keep pulling them up as we mentioned them. And everyone has shown a little bit of a bump for the Democrat in the last several weeks. So Mississippi, South Carolina, quite a big one. Annie Andrews at 28%, which is way higher than she was just a few weeks ago when it was at 13%. No bump at all in Florida. Angie Nixon is at 10%. And that's actually lower than where she was during much of the summer.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，如果你看 Polymarket——因为我们一提它我就一直把它调出来看——过去几周里，几乎每一场都给民主党涨了一点点。比如 Mississippi、South Carolina，涨得还挺大。Annie Andrews 到了 28%，比几周前的 13% 高出很多。而 Florida 一点没涨。Angie Nixon 是 10%，这其实比她整个夏天大部分时候还要低。

turns.en: Yeah, and this follows polling, right? The New York Times had some polling that was very strong for Democrats, but not in Florida. They had Ashley Moody ahead by six or seven or something.
turns.zh: 是啊，这跟民调是吻合的，对吧？New York Times 做过一些民调，对民主党非常有利，但 Florida 除外。他们的民调显示 Ashley Moody 领先 6 到 7 个点之类的。

turns.en: To what degree are prediction markets just like reflecting polling now?
turns.zh: 如今预测市场在多大程度上只是在反映民调？

turns.en: Yeah, talk to us about that.
turns.zh: 是啊，跟我们聊聊这个。

turns.en: I think they're reflecting polling plus sentiment in kind of a, it's somewhere between smart and midwit.
turns.zh: 我觉得它们反映的是民调加上情绪，处在一个……介于'聪明'和'半吊子聪明'（midwit）之间的位置。

turns.en: Right?
turns.zh: 对吧？

turns.en: So again, people in prediction markets do have to quantify ultimately their price, right? And I think that exercise is helpful. When they go play poker, they can be like, oh, I think that guy might be bluffing. I'm saying, I say, well, I'm getting two to one from the pot, right? Last decision I have to make, do I think is a greater than a 33% chance or not? Like, I think the prediction markets have a slightly Republican-leaning clientele, right? Like Democrats are a little preachy about them sometimes. Republicans have more money, right?
turns.zh: 所以说，预测市场里的人最终必须把自己的价格量化出来，对吧？我觉得这个练习是有帮助的。他们去打扑克的时候，会想'哦，我觉得那家伙可能在诈唬（bluffing）'；我会说，嗯，'我从底池（pot）里拿到的是 2 赔 1，对吧；我要做的最后一个决定是——我觉得这是不是大于 33% 的概率'。我觉得预测市场的客户群稍微偏向共和党，对吧？民主党人有时对它们有点说教味儿。共和党人更有钱，对吧？

turns.en: Well, we saw the famous, like, huge whiff in the L.A. mayor race where, like, Spencer Pratt, like, who in their right mind thought a Republican was going to win a mayorship at a major U.S.
turns.zh: 嗯，我们看到了那个著名的、L.A. 市长选举里的大冷门——就是 Spencer Pratt——谁会神志清醒地觉得一个共和党人能赢下美国一个大城市的市长

turns.en: City? Yeah, but, like, they have, like, these, like, the recognition that polling error is correlated, like we talked about at the top of the show. That's an important recognition to have. The markets were actually overconfident relative to my model in 2016 on Hillary Clinton, right? So everyone knows that, but, like, I think The belief that, oh, polls always underestimate Republicans is not the most sophisticated version of that necessarily.
turns.zh: ……之位？是啊，但是，他们有那种——就是我们节目开头聊到的——对'民调误差是相关的'这一点的认识，这是一种很重要的认识。2016 年在 Hillary Clinton 这件事上，市场其实比我的模型更过度自信，对吧？所以这大家都知道，但是，我觉得'哦，民调总是低估共和党'这个信念，未必是这一认识最老练的版本。

turns.en: Is there anyone systematically making money? I mean, I'm going to put you on the spot here or the Silver Bulletin on the spot. But do you feel that someone could make money? betting on prediction markets anytime there's a deviation between silver bulletin model for a given race and the prediction market?
turns.zh: 有没有人在系统性地赚钱？我是说，我要在这儿让你、或者说让 Silver Bulletin 难堪一下了。但你觉得，只要某一场比赛的 Silver Bulletin 模型和预测市场之间出现偏差，就有人能靠在预测市场上下注来赚钱吗？

turns.en: Well, look, I would say when our model came out on August 11th, we moved the markets by several points, right? And so like, if you have markets that can look at our model and are influenced by our model, also look at other models, right? And on top of that, incorporate some degree of vibes. I mean, I helpful. They can also just get to things faster, right? If there's a scandal, the New York times reports, on Thursday morning, then it will take several days to show up in the polling, right? And so like, yeah, I mean, I went through recently and looked at every race where you have a gap between Flipper, my model, and Polymarket. And like, I agree with Polymarket on half of those, you know, although ironically, some of the ones I agreed with, I'm like, oh yeah, Flipper's way too high in South Carolina. And then there's this good poll from South Carolina that brings, you know, so maybe you're kind of arguing it to yourself a little bit, but like, yeah. So the test would be like, you have to create like some type of laboratory environment where prediction markets, aren't allowed to look at polls. And my expectation is that prediction markets would be extremely terrible.
turns.zh: 嗯，你看，我会说，当我们 8 月 11 日模型发布时，我们把市场挪动了好几个点，对吧？所以说，如果你有市场能看我们的模型、并且受我们模型影响，也会去看别的模型，对吧？在此之上，还会掺入一定程度的'感觉'（vibes）。我是说，这有帮助。它们还能更快地反应，对吧？如果爆出一个丑闻，New York Times 在周四早上报道，那它要好几天才会体现在民调里，对吧？所以，是啊，我是说，我最近梳理了一遍，看了每一场 Flipper（我的模型）和 Polymarket 之间有差距的选战。其中有一半我是同意 Polymarket 的，你知道，尽管讽刺的是，有些我同意的，我会想'哦对，Flipper 在 South Carolina 上估得太高了'，然后有一份来自 South Carolina 的好民调把它拉下来，你知道，所以也许你有点在自己跟自己争论，但是，是啊。所以真正的检验应该是：你得造一个实验室式的环境，让预测市场不许看民调。我的预期是，那样一来预测市场会糟糕透顶。

turns.en: Well, it seems like actually the test would be, you would want to have prediction markets that aren't allowed to look at models, right? Because of course they're going to look at- Fair enough. Right? Because ideally you wouldn't want the day the silver bulletin numbers drop to influence the prediction markets. Ideally, you're looking at polls and creating a model and prediction market traders are looking at polls and creating a price- And the question is, which is the better way to derive a probability?
turns.zh: 嗯，其实那个检验似乎应该是：你会想要一个不许看模型的预测市场，对吧？因为它们当然会去看——好吧，说得也是。对吧？因为理想情况下，你不希望 Silver Bulletin 数字发布的那天去影响预测市场。理想情况下，是你看着民调、建一个模型，而预测市场的交易者看着民调、生成一个价格——问题就在于，哪一种是推导出概率的更好方式？

turns.en: Yeah, look, and like building a simulation with all these regional correlations is tricky, right? We are like, as of when we're recording this, we are like literally like 0.995 correlated with polymarket on individual states. We have the overall democratic win probability a bit higher. You know, I don't know if that's because it's attracting a different type of trader, right? Like that, like you get maybe more of the you know, the whales, right? Not like the French whale from 2024, but like whales, like degenerate rich guys with a lot of money to burn, right?
turns.zh: 是啊，你看，而且要建一个包含所有这些地区间相关性的模拟是很棘手的，对吧？截至我们录制的时候，我们在各个州上跟 Polymarket 的相关性简直是 0.995。我们把民主党整体的获胜概率定得稍微高一点。你知道，我不确定那是不是因为它吸引了另一类交易者，对吧？就是你也许会吸引更多那种，你知道，'鲸鱼'（whales，大户），对吧？不是 2024 年那头'法国鲸鱼'，而是那种鲸鱼——就是一帮有钱没处花、乱烧钱的堕落富人，对吧？

turns.en: The dream.
turns.zh: 梦想啊。

turns.en: Whereas they're maybe less likely to invest in individual races. But there's really not that much of a gap, right?
turns.zh: 而他们也许不太会去投单独的一场场选战。但两者之间的差距其实没那么大，对吧？

turns.en: You've been building models for a really long time. And of course, you first sort of became a household name in 2008. So that's 18 years ago.
turns.zh: 你做模型已经做了很久了。当然，你最早算是家喻户晓是在 2008 年，那可是 18 年前了。

turns.en: That's crazy.
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。

turns.en: So that means there are people who are going to be voting in this election that were, like, born during the Obama administration.
turns.zh: 所以这意味着，这次选举里会有一些投票的人，是在 Obama 政府时期出生的。

turns.en: Oh, my gosh. Oh, my God.
turns.zh: 我的天。我的天哪。

turns.en: Some of these things freak me out a little bit. Can you talk objectively about, like, is it unambiguous in your mind that AI has made it easier for you to build models and to do your job?
turns.zh: 有些事情真让我有点发毛。你能客观地聊聊吗——在你心里是否毫无疑问：AI 让你建模、让你做这份工作变得更容易了？

turns.en: Yeah, for sure. Look, I get to hire two world-class programmers, coders, for programming. whatever I pay for the max plans, right? A hundred or 200 bucks a month. So I have these complex projects that you definitely couldn't one shot or even come close to it. But I know this really well and I've quoted these things myself. And I know when you feed GPT or Claude a 10,000 word program and say, carefully audit this, it's quite sharp about it. Now I would still say on like two thirds of prompts, I have to provide quite a bit of guidance, right? It's not like, oh, cool, man. Next step.
turns.zh: 是啊，那当然。你看，我相当于雇到了两个世界级的程序员、编码员——不管我付的是哪个最高档套餐（max plans）的钱，对吧？一个月一百或者两百美元。所以我手上这些复杂的项目，你绝对没法一次成型（one shot），甚至差得远。但我对这块非常熟，我自己也写过这些东西。我知道，当你把一段一万字的程序喂给 GPT 或 Claude，然后说'仔细审查一下这个'，它做得相当敏锐。不过我还是会说，大概三分之二的提示（prompts），我都得提供相当多的引导，对吧？并不是那种'哦，酷，老兄，下一步'。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: But like, it's great. It's a great teammate, you know, to take something in a more obscure example. So we have an NFL model. The NFL has all these complex playoff tiebreakers, right? They're purely algorithmic. And last year when I built our model, it took me two and a half days to code them up. And like some of the code was buggy. We skipped a couple of tiebreakers. It was very slow.
turns.zh: 但是，它很棒。它是个很棒的队友，你知道。举个更冷门的例子。我们有一个 NFL 模型。NFL 有各种复杂的季后赛同分决胜规则（tiebreakers），对吧？它们纯粹是算法性的。去年我建我们这个模型时，光是把这些规则写进代码就花了我两天半。而且有些代码有 bug，我们漏掉了几个决胜规则，非常慢。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: You know, now you have GPT or cloud do it and they do it in 15 minutes while you're at the gym, right? And it's code is 10 times faster. Now, again, there are dangers, like they can introduce bugs and kind of hide them from you. We built a soccer model too. And like in one version of soccer model, it had the ratings like looping back around. So like the 2026 rating would inform like the 1900 rating and it got, it would do things that were, it was quite weird. But you know, the combination of having like a lot of initiative and entrepreneurial spirit and expertise. Cause there's a certain type of person I meet. You guys are probably in that category, right? Where it's like, it's like people are saying me, I feel like I'm the most productive I've ever been.
turns.zh: 你知道，现在你让 GPT 或 Claude 来做，它们在你去健身房的时候，15 分钟就搞定了，对吧？而且代码快 10 倍。当然，风险也是有的，比如它们可能引入 bug，还某种程度上把 bug 藏起来不让你发现。我们也建了一个足球模型。在某个版本的足球模型里，它的评分竟然绕回去了——就是 2026 年的评分会去影响 1900 年的评分，它会做出一些……相当古怪的事。但是，你知道，那种既有大量主动性、又有创业精神和专业能力的组合……因为我会遇到某一类人，你们俩大概也属于那一类，对吧？就是那种，人们跟我说'我觉得我现在是有生以来效率最高的时候'。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I feel like I'm getting two days of work done in, in a 10 hour day sometimes. And I feel like that some of the time, but, but again, I'm probably in the 99.9th percentile of like, these models are helpful with the exact, I'm not really a coder, right? I understand model architecture. I'm an empiricist. I understand probabilities, but like, my coding was always the weak point. So it's like, this exact thing they're really good at and it's really valuable to me is the exact thing that they do very well.
turns.zh: 有时候我觉得自己在 10 小时的工作日里干完了两天的活。我有那么一些时候是这种感觉，但是，再说一次，我大概处在那 99.9 百分位——就是这些模型恰好帮到我的地方。我其实算不上一个程序员，对吧？我懂模型架构，我是个经验主义者（empiricist），我懂概率，但我的编程一直是短板。所以就是，它们特别擅长的这件事、对我特别有价值的这件事，恰恰就是它们做得非常好的那件事。

turns.en: Your FIFA World Cup model did have Spain versus Argentina in the finals.
turns.zh: 你那个 FIFA World Cup（世界杯）模型，确实把决赛预测成了 Spain 对 Argentina。

turns.en: We had a really good, yeah. And that's the thing about, so NFL, you know, you have good weeks and bad weeks and like, that's why, you know, maybe if Republicans win the House, with the Senate, we'd say, well, 25% things happen, right? It'd be great. But like, If they win the house, maybe we'll just make Silver Bulletin AI in a sports blog. Just give up.
turns.zh: 我们表现相当不错，是啊。这就是……说到 NFL，你知道，你有状态好的周也有状态差的周。这就是为什么，你知道，也许如果共和党既赢下众议院又赢下参议院，我们会说'嗯，25% 的概率嘛，什么事都可能发生'，对吧？那会很棒。但是，如果他们赢下众议院，也许我们就干脆把 Silver Bulletin 变成一个 AI 写的体育博客算了。直接放弃。

turns.en: Just give up. Nate Silver, thank you so much for joining us on our Election Day special.
turns.zh: 直接放弃。Nate Silver，非常感谢你来做客我们的选举日特别节目。

turns.en: Thank you, Joe.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Joe。

turns.en: That was a fun conversation, Tracy. I think my favorite part of the conversation... was Nate preemptively parodying how he will sound if Abdul El-Sayed slightly underperforms.
turns.zh: 那场对话很有意思，Tracy。我觉得整场对话里我最喜欢的部分……是 Nate 提前演绎了一波——如果 Abdul El-Sayed 表现稍微低于预期，他自己会是怎么个腔调。

turns.en: It was a good impression of himself. And Nate Silver.
turns.zh: 他模仿自己模仿得挺好。还有 Nate Silver。

turns.en: Doing the impression of an annoying white moderate guy was good. But that was fun. I'm glad. Happy Election Day, people. I'm glad Nate joined us for today. Yeah.
turns.zh: 他模仿那种'讨厌的白人温和派 guy'模仿得很到位。不过那挺有意思的。我很高兴。祝大家选举日快乐。我很高兴 Nate 今天来加入我们。是啊。

turns.en: By the time this comes out, I guess maybe some of the polls will have changed.
turns.zh: 等到这期上线的时候，我猜也许有些民调已经变了。

turns.en: Maybe some of the polls.
turns.zh: 也许有些民调……

turns.en: We'll have some additional.
turns.zh: 我们会有更多……

turns.en: Data, maybe. We'll have some more early voting data.
turns.zh: ……数据，也许。我们会有更多提前投票的数据。

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. One thing I thought was really interesting was this idea of polls basically all becoming models now.
turns.zh: 是啊，正是。我觉得特别有意思的一点，是民调如今基本上都在变成模型这个说法。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And like after years and years and years of being accused of, I guess, overestimating Democrats in the polls, everyone now is self-correcting. And so the question is, like, how big is that self-correction?
turns.zh: 而且，在被指责了这么多年——我猜是在民调里高估民主党——之后，现在人人都在自我修正。所以问题就变成了：这种自我修正的幅度有多大？

turns.en: Yeah. And it's interesting. And I guess we didn't go into the math specifically. But if you can empirically establish that your self-correction here makes no sense.
turns.zh: 嗯。这很有意思。我猜我们没有具体去钻那个数学。但如果能经验上证明，你这里的自我修正是讲不通的……

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: Then what you do learn is, as Nate said, pollsters are self-interested players. Because who is it? What was the famous pollster in Iowa? Seltzer, Ann Seltzer, who actually, you know, right before the 2024 election actually had Kamala Harris winning Iowa. Yeah.
turns.zh: 那么你真正学到的就是，正如 Nate 说的，民调机构是自身利益相关的玩家（self-interested players）。因为那个人是谁来着？Iowa 那位著名的民调专家叫什么？Selzer，Ann Selzer——她在 2024 年选举前，居然给出 Kamala Harris 赢下 Iowa 的结果。是啊。

turns.en: No one wants to poll a Seltzer, right?
turns.zh: 没人想弄出 Selzer 那样的民调结果，对吧？

turns.en: It was so off that she retired from the game. And that's kind of, I guess, what Nate was saying, too, which is that if Republicans win the House, it's like, you know what, I think we're done. I think we're done trying to go into sports. These crazy American voters. We're done trying to understand anything about them because we have nothing. We have no usable information on them. Go ask your digital twin.
turns.zh: 那份民调错得太离谱，她直接退出了这一行。我想这大概也正是 Nate 说的：如果共和党赢下众议院，那就等于说'你知道吗，我觉得我们完了。我觉得我们不干了，转去做体育。这些疯狂的美国选民——我们不干了，不再试图去理解他们的任何事，因为我们什么都没有，我们手上没有任何关于他们的可用信息。去问你的数字孪生吧。'

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好了。

turns.en: Shall we leave it there?
turns.zh: 我们就聊到这儿吧？

turns.en: Yeah, let's leave it there.
turns.zh: 好，就聊到这儿。
